notes: Ruling slot 23 = House of Bolkiah (Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah). Partai Rakyat Brunei, banned and in exile since 1962, placed in non-aligned socialist slot 18 (has popularity). Omar Ali Saifuddien III's circle resisting British pressure for democratisation fills reactionary slot 6. Sultan moved out of MD slot 12 into 23; regiment kept in 22. Shia, jihadist and several small slots are invented catchy circles without named persons.

0.name: British High Commission in Brunei
0.text:
Under the 1959 Agreement the British High Commissioner in Brunei handles the sultanate's defence and foreign relations, while the Gurkha battalion stationed in the Seria oilfields since the 1962 revolt guarantees its security. London has spent the 1960s urging the palace toward elected government and, failing that, toward joining Malaysia.

The High Commission wants a stable, pro-Western Brunei that protects Shell's oil, keeps communism out of northern Borneo and gradually democratises. Its leverage is the British military presence, control of external affairs and the threat of withdrawing protection, though the palace has learned to resist its advice with growing confidence.

1.name: Majlis Mesyuarat Negeri
1.text:
The Legislative Council was created by the 1959 Constitution. After the Partai Rakyat landslide of 1962 was cancelled by the revolt, the 1965 elections returned members loyal to the palace, and the Council now combines elected, nominated and official members under the Sultan's emergency powers.

Its members are district notables, senior civil servants and businessmen who favour cautious constitutional progress, British protection and loyalty to the throne. They oppose both the banned left and union with Malaysia on Kuala Lumpur's terms. Their leverage is limited to debate and budget scrutiny, but they are the only channel through which ordinary Bruneians are represented at all.

2.name: Barisan Kemerdekaan Rakyat
2.text:
Barisan Kemerdekaan Rakyat was formed in the mid-1960s by Bruneian nationalists seeking a legal path to self-government after the ban on Partai Rakyat. It is tolerated but tightly constrained by the state of emergency, and its activists are watched by the police Special Branch.

The Front calls for full independence from Britain, a fully elected legislature, a constitutional monarchy and civil liberties, while rejecting armed struggle and incorporation into Malaysia. It draws on teachers, clerks and young townspeople in Brunei Town and Kuala Belait. Its leverage lies in the widespread memory of the 1962 vote and in British pressure on the palace to democratise.

3.name: Pekerja Minyak Seria
3.text:
The oil workers of Seria and Kuala Belait are the only real industrial working class in Brunei, employed by Brunei Shell or its contractors and organised in cautious staff associations and unions. Many supported Partai Rakyat in 1962, and since the revolt their organisations have stayed strictly within the law.

They seek better wages, housing, pensions and localisation of skilled jobs held by expatriates, and they want a share of oil revenue spent on schools and clinics. They are reformist rather than revolutionary and have no outside patron. Their leverage lies in the oilfield itself: a stoppage at Seria would cut off almost all of the sultanate's income.

4.name: Sel Merah Kuala Belait
4.text:
The Red Cells are small study groups of Chinese and Malay workers and students in Kuala Belait and Seria, linked by couriers to the communist underground across the border in Sarawak. They have no public leaders; most members are known only to the police by their informers' code names.

The cells read Marxist classics, circulate smuggled pamphlets and dream of a workers' state in a united North Kalimantan, free of the sultan, Shell and the British. They are too weak to fight and avoid open action. Their leverage lies in grievances over pay and citizenship among the oilfield Chinese, many of whom remain stateless.

5.name: Tentera Nasional Kalimantan Utara
5.text:
The TNKU was the armed wing of Partai Rakyat Brunei that launched the revolt of December 1962, seizing police stations and the Seria oilfield before British and Gurkha troops crushed it within days. Its field commander Yassin Affandi was captured, and its surviving fighters are dead, imprisoned or scattered in Indonesia.

The remnant still dreams of a unitary North Kalimantan state uniting Brunei, Sarawak and Sabah under a constitutional sultan and a people's government. It rejects British protection and Malaysia alike. Its leverage today is almost entirely symbolic: the prisoners held without trial and the memory of a rising that briefly shook the sultanate.

6.name: Golongan Seri Begawan
6.text:
The Seri Begawan Circle gathers around Omar Ali Saifuddien III, who abdicated in 1967 in favour of his son but remains the dominant figure behind the throne. Around him stand courtiers, religious officials and senior pengiran who resent British pressure to introduce elected government.

The circle regards democracy as a foreign imposition that nearly destroyed the sultanate in 1962. It wants to preserve absolute royal authority, Malay custom and Islam, refuse Malaysian federation and reduce British interference to the bare minimum needed for defence. Its leverage lies in the former sultan's prestige, his control over palace appointments and the young Sultan's deference to his father.

7.name: Jalur Jakarta
7.text:
The Jakarta Line is a loose network of Bruneian officials, former Partai Rakyat sympathisers and traders who look to Indonesia as the natural patron of a free Borneo. It survives through contacts in Jakarta, where exiles from the 1962 revolt still live, and through quiet sympathy among some Malay officers and civil servants.

The network wants British troops gone and a strong, nationalist Malay state allied with Indonesia rather than the West. Since Suharto ended Confrontation it has lost its official backing, but it keeps its hopes alive. Its leverage lies in cross-border family ties, smuggling routes through Kalimantan and the possibility that Jakarta's interest might revive.

8.name: Jemaah Ahlul Bait Brunei
8.text:
The Ahlul Bait Fellowship is a handful of Bruneian students and South Asian traders who have encountered Shia teachings abroad and meet discreetly in private homes. Brunei's official Islam is strictly Sunni and Shafi'i, regulated by the Religious Council, and the group keeps its existence quiet.

Its members stress love for the family of the Prophet, reasoned scholarship and the duty of rulers toward the poor. They avoid politics and confrontation with the palace, preferring education and charity. Their leverage is negligible, resting only on overseas contacts and the curiosity of a few young people trained in Arabic at foreign universities.

9.name: Pemuda Karbala Brunei
9.text:
Pemuda Karbala is a tiny secret circle of young Bruneians radicalised by the Shia clergy of Iraq during their studies abroad. It has no known leader, no publications and only a few members, all of whom would face detention if discovered.

The circle sees the sultanate's oil wealth, British protection and courtly luxury as an affront to Islamic justice and dreams of rule by learned clergy. It rejects both the West and atheist communism. Its leverage is close to nothing, resting on zeal alone and on the hope that a wider religious awakening in the Muslim world will one day reach Borneo.

10.name: Majlis Ugama Islam Brunei
10.text:
The Brunei Islamic Religious Council was created under Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien III to administer Islamic law, mosques, religious schools, zakat and the conduct of Muslims. The Sultan is its head as the supreme authority of Islam in the state, and its officials are among the most respected members of the administration.

The Council upholds Sunni Shafi'i orthodoxy, loyalty to the ruler and the integration of religion into state life. It supports the monarchy against secular radicals and communists and maintains ties with Al-Azhar and the Saudi religious establishment. Its leverage lies in mosques in every kampung, religious education and royal backing.

11.name: Darul Islam Borneo
11.text:
Darul Islam Borneo is a clandestine fraternity inspired by the Darul Islam rebellion of West Java and by pamphlets of the global caliphate movement. Its few members are religious teachers and students who meet in private and have no publicly known leader.

The fraternity holds that sultans, colonial agreements and secular parties are illegitimate and that Borneo's Muslims must be united in a single Islamic state as part of a restored caliphate. It rejects both British protection and Malaysian federalism. Its leverage is tiny but its ideas circulate among students returning from abroad and in remote kampung where state religious officials rarely visit.

12.name: Angkatan Dakwah Brunei
12.text:
Angkatan Dakwah is a network of young religious teachers and graduates of Egyptian and Malaysian institutions who admire the Muslim Brotherhood and the Malaysian Islamic Party across the border. It runs study circles and Quran classes and has no formal leader.

The network wants public life, education and law reshaped according to Islamic principles through preaching, welfare and gradual reform, not revolt. It criticises corruption, Western entertainment and the influence of foreign oil men. Its leverage lies in its moral authority among young Malays and its potential to channel the frustrations of a generation denied open party politics.

13.name: Majlis Mesyuarat Menteri-Menteri
13.text:
The Council of Ministers is the executive body created by the 1959 Constitution, chaired by the Sultan and run day to day by the Menteri Besar, Pengiran Muhammad Yusuf. Under the emergency powers in force since 1962, it governs with little reference to the legislature.

The Council is staffed by senior Malay officials and pengiran who manage oil revenue, the civil service, housing schemes and development plans. It prefers administration to politics, avoids alignment beyond British protection and seeks to buy loyalty through welfare. Its leverage lies in controlling the budget, appointments and the state's growing oil income.

14.name: Majlis Wazir
14.text:
The Wazirs are the great officers of state of the Brunei court, such as the Pengiran Bendahara and Pengiran Pemancha, drawn from the royal nobility and supported by the cheteria and the hereditary chiefs of the kampung. Their titles date back centuries and they still preside over ceremony, custom and many local disputes.

They defend a hierarchical society of ruler, nobles and commoners, Malay custom and Islam. They are neither pro-British nor anti-British, but suspicious of parties, unions and elections that threaten their status. Their leverage lies in tradition, royal kinship, land and the authority of village headmen who answer to them.

15.name: Brunei Shell Petroleum
15.text:
Brunei Shell Petroleum is the operating company of the Shell group in the sultanate, producing oil from the Seria field since 1929 and now drilling offshore. Its revenues pay for nearly everything the state spends, and its expatriate managers form a powerful community in Seria and Kuala Belait.

The company wants stable royal government, British protection, low labour costs and no nationalisation. It quietly funds roads, schools and hospitals to preserve goodwill. Its leverage is overwhelming: the oil revenue that underwrites the sultanate's welfare state, and the technical knowledge without which production would collapse.

16.name: Brunei Chinese Chamber of Commerce
16.text:
The Chinese Chamber of Commerce speaks for the shopkeepers, contractors, importers and timber traders who dominate commerce in Brunei Town and the oil towns. Many Chinese residents remain without Bruneian citizenship and cannot own land freely, so the chamber is their main channel to the authorities.

It favours open trade, low taxes and a light-handed state, and lobbies quietly for citizenship and property rights rather than political power. It is anti-communist and wary of radicals among Chinese youth. Its leverage lies in its control of retail and construction and the state's dependence on Chinese skills and capital.

17.name: Penjaga Hutan Temburong
17.text:
The Temburong Forest Keepers are a loose group of foresters, teachers and Iban and Murut villagers in the isolated Temburong district who want its rainforest left intact. They have no formal leadership and work through the forestry service and community elders.

They argue that Brunei's oil wealth makes logging unnecessary and that the forests, rivers and mangroves of Temburong and Kampong Ayer must be protected for future generations. They avoid politics and Cold War alignments. Their leverage is limited, but the state's lack of need for timber revenue gives their case a sympathetic hearing in the forestry department.

18.name: Partai Rakyat Brunei
18.text:
Partai Rakyat Brunei was founded in 1956 by A. M. Azahari and won every elected seat in the 1962 District Council elections. When the sultanate moved toward Malaysia and the Legislative Council was not convened, its armed wing launched the December 1962 revolt; the party was banned and Azahari has lived in exile in Indonesia ever since.

The party stands for independence, parliamentary democracy under a constitutional sultan, land reform and a unitary North Kalimantan state. It is non-aligned and anti-colonial, rejecting both British protection and Malaysia. Its leverage is the lasting popularity it enjoyed in 1962 and its many members still held without trial.

19.name: Jalur Paraku
19.text:
The Paraku Line is a small network of Bruneian supporters of the North Kalimantan People's Army, the communist guerrillas fighting in neighbouring Sarawak. It consists mostly of Chinese youth from Chinese-medium schools and a few former Partai Rakyat radicals, and it has no public leader.

The network follows Maoist doctrine: armed struggle from the countryside, a people's democratic North Kalimantan and alignment with Beijing against both Washington and Moscow. It provides couriers, safe houses and funds rather than fighters. Its leverage lies in the porous border with Sarawak and the frustrations of stateless Chinese residents in the oil towns.

20.name: Angkatan Kebangsaan Melayu Brunei
20.text:
The Malay National Front is a movement of Malay clerks, teachers and petty traders who resent the dominance of Chinese commerce, expatriate managers and British officials. It works through youth clubs, mosques and the teachers' associations, and has no single recognised leader.

It demands that jobs, land, licences and citizenship be reserved for Malays, that expatriates be replaced by Bruneians and that the sultanate never be absorbed by Malaysia. It is loyal to the throne but impatient with the courtiers. Its leverage lies in genuine resentment among the Malay majority and its ability to mobilise crowds in Brunei Town.

21.name: Panglima Sabil
21.text:
The Panglima Sabil are a secretive brotherhood of silat masters, former auxiliaries from the 1962 emergency and young Malay militants who invoke the warrior tradition of the old Brunei empire. They train in remote kampung and have no known leader.

They preach the armed defence of Malay race, Islam and sultan against communists, Chinese, Christians and foreign interference, and dream of a restored Brunei empire over northern Borneo. They despise parties and elections. Their leverage is small, but they could become a dangerous street force if the authorities ever turn to them against the left.

22.name: Askar Melayu Diraja Brunei
22.text:
The Brunei Malay Regiment was founded in 1961 and received its royal title in 1965. It is a small force of a few hundred Malay soldiers, trained and partly officered by British seconded personnel, and is being expanded with oil revenue alongside the Gurkha battalion based at Seria.

The regiment's loyalty is to the Sultan personally, and it sees its task as preventing another 1962. It is anti-communist and dependent on British training, equipment and advice. Its leverage lies in being the only Bruneian armed force, giving its officers access to the palace and a growing role in internal security.

23.name: House of Bolkiah
23.text:
The House of Bolkiah has ruled Brunei for more than six centuries. Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah succeeded in October 1967 when his father, Omar Ali Saifuddien III, abdicated, and was crowned in August 1968; he governs by decree under emergency powers in force since the 1962 revolt.

The dynasty defends royal sovereignty, Malay custom and Islam, refuses to join Malaysia and resists British pressure for a fully elected government. Oil revenue lets it fund free schooling, health care and housing in exchange for political loyalty. Its leverage is near-total: the treasury, the regiment, religious authority and the deep attachment of most Malays to the throne.
